comments.author: ilitirit
comments.text:
I've all but given up on these types of approaches. Models will often just ignore your process instructions at the most inopportune moments. For work, I've resorted to mostly just using single agents for smallish pieces of work that I orchestrate myself. I treat it as a tool, with me being the craftsman.
Everyone is pushing Agent Fleets and Swarms, and I'm sure that there are many success stories, but from our internal experiments many devs don't see any speed advantage for complex work. Here's what one of them told us recently: "The speed advantage is offset by the manual refactoring work. The code is 'correct', but it's just not what any of us would have written".
Now one could argue that you could just ignore the code if it's working (that is in fact what Ex Co instructed us to do) and just keep running these fleets if the end result "works", but I'm not fully convinced this will end well in the long term.
Then again, I'm stuck with decades of legacy code and systems that noone understands that were introduced by humans...

comments.text:
The article (which seems to be from 2026-04-24 based on its URL) refers to the JDK 26 version of the PEM Encodings API. [1]
[1]:
https://openjdk.org/jeps/524
The article points out a potential pitfall with how this version of the API exposes a sealed class. If the application has an exhaustive switch expression that lists all permitted subclasses, and a later JDK release were to add a new permitted subclass, this would potentially expose the application to a MatchException at runtime.
In the JDK 27 version of the PEM Encodings API, JEP 538 [2], we’ve adjusted the permitted subclasses of the sealed class in question to include a non-public permitted subclass.
[2]:
https://openjdk.org/jeps/538
This prevents applications from using an exhaustive switch expression by enumerating all permitted subclasses. This allows the JDK to extend set of permitted subclasses in the future without exposing applications to the risk of unexpected exceptions.

stories.title_en: A new way to think about borrow checking (in reverse)

comments.author: verdagon
comments.text:
Figuring out how to make this was a pretty wild ride. I had zero clue how to approach this, so I went into the mountains with pencil and paper until I figured something out.
I started with a sort of "compile-time generational references" approach, where every reference would also remember
when
it was made, at compile-time. Then that evolved into a couple more things until I finally figured out this reverse approach. We'll see if it sticks.
Hope you all enjoy!

comments.author: Animats
comments.text:
Interesting.
In Hoare-type proof of correctness work, it's normal to work backwards from the proof goal (such as an assert statement) back upwards through the program, adding info about code that affects the variables in the assertion. This approach to borrow checking follows that model. You want some state at some point, and you work backwards to see if the preceding code gets you there. Makes a lot of sense for lifetimes.
The main problem with doing this inside a compiler is performance. You backtrack for each thing you need to prove, going through the same code more than once. I used to think that compilers should use more verification technology, but people start screaming about compile times.
